strengths: Addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: relation hallucinations in LVLMs.
Proposes a training-free method that is model-agnostic and can be applied to different LVLM architectures.
Combines multiple components—text-guided attention enhancement, multi-perspective question decomposition, and interleaved text-image reasoning with visual memory—into a coherent pipeline.
Reports consistent improvements over vanilla and two baselines (Constraint-Aware Prompting, Detect-then-Calibrate) on MMRel and R-Bench across LLaVA-1.5 and InstructBLIP.
Includes ablation studies and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis that provide some insight into module contributions and parameter choices.
Qualitative case studies and attention-map visualizations help illustrate the intended reasoning process.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method largely aggregates existing ideas such as prompt decomposition, interleaved chain-of-thought, text-guided attention, and attention manipulation, with only incremental adaptation to relation hallucination.
Evaluation is narrow: only two relatively old 7B LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5 and InstructBLIP) and two relation-focused benchmarks are used; no recent LVLMs or broader multimodal benchmarks are evaluated.

Improvements are small and often within a few points: e.g., LLaVA on R-Bench improves accuracy by only 0.18% over prompting, and InstructBLIP on MMRel improves accuracy by 0.62% over prompting; no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported.
Baseline comparisons are limited and may be reimplemented under unclear settings; no comparison to more recent relation-hallucination or general hallucination-mitigation methods.

Method details are under-specified: extraction of the relation component [R] from arbitrary questions is not explained, final integration of accumulated visual memory into the original-question answer is unclear, and attention-modification implementation across architectures lacks reproducibility details.
Ablated variants all still outperform the vanilla baseline, suggesting that gains may come from generic prompting/context effects rather than the proposed visual-memory mechanism specifically.
Hyperparameter sensitivity appears high, with performance dropping substantially at larger k_max and lambda values, yet selection is only validated on one model and one dataset.
Efficiency trade-offs are not analyzed: inference is reported to be about 4x slower, which may limit practical applicability.
Writing and referencing contain inconsistencies (e.g., typos, citation-year mismatches) and important implementation details such as prompt templates and keyword/relation extraction are missing.

strengths: Addresses an important but relatively under-explored problem: relation hallucinations in large vision-language models.
Proposes a training-free approach that avoids expensive fine-tuning and can in principle be applied to different white-box LVLMs.
The subject-object-relation decomposition and multi-perspective question construction are intuitive and inspired by human relational reasoning.
Uses both textual memory and visual attention memory across reasoning steps, and the ablation attempts to isolate contributions of each module.
Evaluates on two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel and R-Bench) and two LVLMs, with sensitivity analysis and qualitative case studies.
The case studies and attention visualizations provide some qualitative evidence that the method changes model focus toward task-relevant regions.
weaknesses: A central technical formula is problematic: Eq. (1) computes V' from V (dimension d_v) and X (dimension d_t), which requires d_v = d_t for V X^T and outputs a d_t-dimensional representation, yet V' is subsequently treated as enhanced visual tokens. No projection or dimension correction is described, making the core text-guided attention module unclear and potentially invalid as written.

Reproducibility is weak: no code, no exact question templates, no specification of the spaCy model, keyword extraction details, attention head/layer aggregation, top-k mask construction, or how attention bias is injected into LLaVA and InstructBLIP.
The confidence term Conf_prev_i in Eq. (5) is not defined, even though it controls the strength of the visual attention bias and is central to the interleaved chain.

The proposed visual memory can propagate errors: attention masks are derived from earlier answers, so an incorrect early sub-answer can bias later attention and reinforce the hallucination rather than correct it.

Evaluation is limited: only two 7B models are tested, and gains are modest without statistical significance testing or error bars. For example, on InstructBLIP MMRel, the improvement over the prompting baseline is only 0.62 accuracy points.

Baselines are limited to two methods and are reimplemented without sufficient tuning or implementation details. Many other hallucination-mitigation approaches, including contrastive decoding, self-correction, and relation-specific methods, are not compared.

Ablations are only reported for LLaVA-1.5 on MMRel, not across both benchmarks and models, and there is no per-category breakdown for spatial, action, and comparative relations despite relation type being central.
The main results report precision but not recall, so it is difficult to tell whether improvements come from reducing false positives, false negatives, or both.

Novelty is incremental: the method combines existing ideas such as chain-of-thought prompting, cross-attention enhancement, and attention biasing, but does not establish a clear fundamental advance over prior prompting or calibration methods.
The 'interleaved text-image reasoning chain' framing is somewhat overstated: the image itself is not updated; only attention biases over the same visual tokens are propagated across steps.
Practical applicability is limited to white-box LVLMs because the method requires modifying internal attention maps and accessing hidden states during decoding.

strengths: Addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: relation hallucinations in LVLMs, which account for a large share of hallucination errors but receive less attention than object/attribute hallucinations.
The proposed ChainMPQ is training-free and model-agnostic, making it easy to apply to off-the-shelf LVLMs without fine-tuning.
The method has a clear structure: text-guided attention enhancement, multi-perspective question decomposition, and interleaved text-image reasoning with accumulated textual/visual memory.
Experiments show consistent improvements across two LVLMs (LLaVA-1.5 and InstructBLIP) and two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel and R-Bench).
Ablation studies provide useful evidence for the three core modules, and case studies with attention maps qualitatively illustrate the intended progressive reasoning process.
The paper is generally well motivated and connects to prior work on chain-of-thought and interleaved multimodal reasoning.
weaknesses: The reported improvements are modest in several settings, e.g., only +0.18 accuracy on R-Bench with LLaVA-1.5 and +0.62 accuracy on MMRel with InstructBLIP over the best prompting baseline, with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

The evaluation is limited in scope: only two LVLMs, two relation benchmarks, and two relation-specific baselines; there is no comparison to standard chain-of-thought, ICoT, or more general hallucination-mitigation decoding strategies.
Recall is not reported, despite precision and F1 being included; the claim of reduced false positives without sacrificing recall is therefore not directly verifiable.

Several technical details are unclear or potentially problematic, including how cross-attention is computed when visual and text feature dimensions may differ, exactly which layers are modified, and how the attention bias is integrated during autoregressive generation.
The method relies on NLP keyword/relation extraction and constructed sub-questions; errors in these steps can propagate through the chain, but no error analysis or robustness study is provided.
Reproducibility is limited: no code is released, and implementation details such as exact prompts, attention extraction, and baseline re-implementation are not sufficiently specified.
The computational overhead is not negligible (roughly 4x inference time), and sensitivity to key hyperparameters such as k_max and lambda is not fully analyzed.
The qualitative case studies are illustrative but not a substitute for broader quantitative analysis; human evaluation or a more detailed failure analysis is missing.
Some claims, such as 'substantially reduces relation hallucinations,' are stronger than the evidence supports given the modest and mixed benchmark gains.
The paper has writing/formatting issues and some inconsistent or incorrect references, which affect clarity and polish.

strengths: Addresses the under-explored problem of relation hallucinations in LVLMs with a training-free, model-agnostic framework.

The core idea of decomposing a relational question into subject/object/relation-focused sub-questions and chaining them with textual and visual memory is reasonable and motivated by prior CoT/ICoT work.

Evaluates ChainMPQ on four LVLMs and two relation-focused benchmarks, showing consistent improvements over several baselines, and includes latency/performance trade-off experiments plus general benchmark results in the appendix.
Provides ablation studies for the three main components and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis for k_max and lambda, which helps validate the design to some extent.
Includes qualitative case studies and attention visualizations that illustrate how the method can shift focus toward relation-relevant regions.
weaknesses: The text-guided cross-attention formulation in Eq. 1 is technically unclear and appears dimensionally inconsistent: it multiplies an image feature matrix by a text feature matrix without specifying any projection, normalization, or how the output remains in the visual token space.

The interleaved attention-memory equations (Eqs. 2-6) are ambiguous: M_i is defined over visual tokens but added to an attention logit matrix over likely all tokens, and the shape alignment is not explained. It is also unclear whether Attn_i is cross-attention, self-attention, averaged over heads, or how keyword-token indices are aligned across decoder layers.

The confidence term Conf_prev_i and the resulting alpha_i in Eq. 5 are never defined or computed. This is a central part of the proposed visual memory propagation, making the method difficult to reproduce and evaluate rigorously.

Novelty is limited: the method largely combines existing ingredients (chain-of-thought prompting, multi-perspective question decomposition, attention intervention, and ICoT-style interleaving) with rule-based masking and GPT-3.5-based question refinement; there is no fundamentally new mechanism or theoretical insight.

Empirical gains are modest in several settings, e.g., LLaVA-1.5 on R-Bench improves only from 75.86 to 76.04 accuracy over the strongest prompting baseline, and InternVL3.5 improves by about 1.08 accuracy. No variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

The evaluation is narrow: only MMRel and image-level R-Bench are used, with two main relation-specific baselines plus CoT. The paper does not compare against Triplet Description (Wu et al., 2025b / Tri-HE), which is discussed in related work and is directly relevant to relation hallucinations.

Ablations are conducted only with LLaVA-1.5 on MMRel, so generalization of the component analysis across models, benchmarks, and relation categories is unsupported. There is also no separate ablation of confidence weighting, entropy-adaptive top-k, layer n, or text memory versus visual memory beyond the coarse w/o variants.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or implementation details for the confidence metric, attention extraction, GPT-3.5 Turbo prompts, spaCy version, or hyperparameter selection protocol are provided. The hyperparameters k_max and lambda appear tuned on the same MMRel benchmark used for evaluation.

The attention-memory mechanism can propagate earlier errors: if a sub-question produces a confidently wrong answer, the top-k visual memory bias is likely to reinforce incorrect regions rather than correct them, and the paper provides no safeguard or causal correction mechanism.

Claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence, e.g., 'substantially reduces relation hallucinations' despite small accuracy improvements in some settings, and the notation is dense enough that key steps are hard to verify.

strengths: Addresses relation hallucination in LVLMs, an important and relatively understudied problem compared to object and attribute hallucinations.
Training-free and model-agnostic, with experiments across four LVLMs of different architectures (LLaVA, InstructBLIP, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3.5).
The high-level idea is intuitive: decompose relational questions into subject/object/relation perspectives and use textual plus visual memory across reasoning steps.
Evaluates on two relation-focused benchmarks (MMRel and R-Bench) and includes additional general benchmarks (MMBench/MME) plus ablations and latency analysis in the appendix.
Reports consistent improvements over baselines across models and benchmarks, with some precision gains on R-Bench.
Provides qualitative case studies and attention visualizations that help illustrate the intended reasoning behavior.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is largely an engineering combination of existing ideas such as prompt decomposition, interleaved multimodal chain-of-thought, top-k attention masks, and attention bias injection. No fundamentally new technique or insight is introduced.

The improvements are often marginal. For example, on R-Bench with LLaVA-1.5, accuracy improves from 75.86 (best baseline) to 76.04 (+0.18), and with InternVL3.5 from 83.97 to 85.05 (+1.08). No statistical significance tests or error bars are reported, and the abstract's claim of substantially reducing hallucinations is overstated.

Missing important baselines: Triplet Description (Wu et al., 2025b), ICoT (Gao et al., 2025) which directly inspired this work, and other recent relation-hallucination mitigation methods are not compared. This undermines the empirical positioning.

Technical details are unclear and potentially inconsistent. Eq. (1) uses V in R^{M x d_v} and X in R^{N x d_t}, but V' = softmax(V X^T) X has dimension d_t, not d_v, unless d_t = d_v. No projection or dimension alignment is explained.

Critical variables are undefined: Conf_prev_i and how confidence is computed; how the attention bias M_i is injected into decoder self-attention (which layers, only visual tokens, how dimensions align); and how keyword token indices T are selected from question tokens.

Eq. (6) sums previous visual biases from j=3 to i, so for i=3 the sum is empty, which conflicts with Algorithm 2's use of M_i for Q3. The timing and scope of bias application across Q3-Q5 are not clearly specified.

The entropy-based adaptive k in Eq. (3) is not well justified. It is unclear why high-entropy attention should select many visual tokens, or how this avoids including irrelevant regions while preserving necessary context.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code release, missing implementation details for attention extraction and bias injection, unclear use of GPT-3.5 Turbo for question refinement, and limited description of baseline reimplementation.

Evaluation is limited: only two relation benchmarks are used, and R-Bench is evaluated only at the image level. No variance across random seeds, no statistical testing, and no analysis of failure cases beyond a few qualitative examples.

Ablation results show that the text-guided attention enhancement contributes only 1.14% accuracy on MMRel, suggesting limited benefit relative to its complexity. The multi-perspective and interleaved components contribute more, but still modestly.
Inference cost is high: full ChainMPQ takes 3.3s/sample versus 0.9s for vanilla LLaVA, and even Light1 takes 1.5s. Latency is not compared against the baseline methods.

The method introduces many hyperparameters and external dependencies (k_max, lambda, n, spaCy, GPT-3.5 refinement), but sensitivity analysis is limited to k_max and lambda, and robustness across models/datasets is not fully established.

strengths: Addresses the underexplored problem of relation hallucinations in LVLMs with a training-free, model-agnostic approach.
Combines text-guided attention enhancement, multi-perspective question decomposition, and an interleaved text-image reasoning chain in a conceptually intuitive pipeline.
Evaluates the method on four representative LVLMs and two relation-focused benchmarks, showing consistent improvements in accuracy, precision, and F1.
Includes ablation studies, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, qualitative case studies, and attention visualizations to support the design choices.
Provides useful implementation details such as spaCy keyword extraction, hyperparameter settings, baseline reproduction, and additional MMBench/MME results in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the method integrates existing ideas such as CoT prompting, multi-perspective question decomposition, attention calibration, and top-k visual bias, without a clear conceptual breakthrough.

Technical formulation is unclear or potentially flawed in places: Eq. 1 assumes visual and text feature dimensions match without projection, the confidence term Conf_prev_i in Eq. 5 is not defined, and the k_max setting is inconsistent (20 vs. 10% of patches).
The method relies on external tools (spaCy and GPT-3.5 Turbo for question refinement), which weakens the 'training-free' claim and raises reproducibility, cost, and robustness concerns.

Evaluation is limited to two yes/no relation benchmarks and misses comparison to other recent relation-hallucination methods such as Triplet Description/Tri-HE; no significance testing or error bars are provided.

Empirical gains are modest in several settings (e.g., LLaVA on R-Bench: 76.04 vs. 75.86 accuracy; InternVL3.5 on MMRel: 75.21 vs. 74.45), making claims of 'substantially reducing' relation hallucinations seem overstated.
Baselines are limited to vanilla CoT and two training-free methods; broader comparisons and failure-case analyses are missing.
The efficiency analysis shows full ChainMPQ is 3.3 s/sample vs. 0.9 s/sample for vanilla, which may limit practical deployment despite Light variants.
The main paper lacks important implementation details, especially how multi-perspective questions are generated/refined in practice and how previous-answer confidence is computed.
